title: The Resistance to Non-Perfect Memory Mapping: Psychological Inertia Against Interference Effects
text:
Scientific evidence demonstrates that recall is rarely a clean process, making subjects susceptible to interference—the degradation of memory retrieval capacity due to exposure to other information. Despite rigorous neurocognitive models proving the quantifiable nature of this decay and crossover effect (a measure linked to underlying plasticity failure), there exists significant psychological inertia in accepting these limitations.

This resistance mirrors the 'fixed ability' mythos: many educational, therapeutic, and self-improvement paradigms are founded on an assumption of perfect memory encoding or a simple, linear accumulation of skills. The concept of susceptibility—that relearning or new learning can actively degrade previously achieved proficiency (retroactive interference)—is often met with cultural denial or deep cognitive discomfort.

The willingness to accept that mastery is transient and context-dependent requires a profound shift away from the idealized view of the permanent intellect, creating sociological resistance even when highly accurate data disprove the presumed stability of knowledge structures.
